$comment: What agentlings may reach outside their sandbox. A connection declares its
own default with 'defaultOn'; the user's departures from those defaults are
recorded in .agentlings/settings.json, never here. Secrets are named, never
written here — put the value in .env under that name and the server passes
it to the connection only. A connection whose secrets are missing is never
live, whatever its default says.
'web' is built in and defaultOn: this is an outreach platform, so reaching
a page is what the crew is for rather than something to be asked for job by
job. Switch it off in Settings. It is our own fetch, which returns readable
text trimmed to maxChars rather than a whole page. Add hosts to 'allow' to
narrow it.
Every connection lists the 'tools' a job may call on it. The list is the
grant: a server offering both reading and acting can be adopted for
reading alone by naming only its reading tools, and anything not named is
refused by the allowlist. It also makes this file say what a connection
can do without anyone having to run it.
'browser' is Playwright MCP (Apache-2.0, Microsoft), fetched by npx so no
code lands in this repo. It is deliberately READ-ONLY: of the 24 tools it
offers, the eight named below read a page and none of them act. Left out
on purpose are click, type, fill_form, press_key, select_option, drag,
drop, file_upload, handle_dialog, evaluate, run_code_unsafe and
network_request — because this app's safety model is a sandbox reviewed
before anything is promoted, and a submitted form cannot be reviewed
afterwards. Adding an acting tool is a decision about that model, not a
line in a list.
It signs in by re-using a session you created yourself: log in once in a
real browser, save the storage state, and point AGENTLINGS_BROWSER_STATE
at the file. The app never sees a password — and with the variable unset
the argument is dropped and browsing works signed out.
'github' is builtin rather than an MCP server, and that is a decision
(D-040). The reference GitHub MCP server is deprecated by npm, and the
supported replacement ships as Docker or a remote HTTP endpoint that this
registry cannot express. Builtin is the better answer regardless, for the
reason given below about stdio budgets: a code host is exactly where an
unbounded reply hurts, since one issue list or one diff can be enormous.
Owning the call means owning the size of the answer, so every tool returns
compact lines and none of them returns a patch. It reads and cannot act:
of the 26 tools the reference server exposes, the 12 that create, update,
comment, merge, push or fork are absent, and catalog.test.ts asserts it.
It needs GITHUB_TOKEN in .env and is never live without one.
'search' is builtin for the same reason as 'github', and exists because of
a measured failure (D-053): the crew could read a page you named and never
find one, and a missing capability is substituted rather than refused — one
run answered from model knowledge and said so, another spent its whole
budget driving the browser at a search engine and died. A search API answers
in verbose JSON, so owning the call owns the size: what comes back is three
fields a result, enough to choose a URL and hand it to fetch_page. The two
tools compose and both trim. It needs BRAVE_API_KEY in .env and is never
live without one; it ships off, like everything credentialed.
Brave rather than Google, and that is not a preference — Google Custom
Search stopped being a general web search on 20 January 2026. Engines
created after that date can only search up to 50 domains you nominate, and
existing whole-web engines lose it on 1 January 2027. It was built against
Google first and reverted when the console refused to enable the toggle
(D-054). Scraping the search page is not the fallback: it is against the
terms, and D-035 measured what it returns to a crawler anyway — 429 and a
CAPTCHA, which is the wall the run in D-053 died against.
External MCP servers take: name, label, description, transport 'stdio',
command, args, tools, and optional secrets {ENV_NAME: 'why it is needed'}.
They ship off by default — they carry credentials and act on the user's
behalf, which is a different decision from reading a page. Keep results
small by design — every token a tool returns is a token the model pays to
read, and for a stdio server that budget is the server's own flags, not
ours: the SDK talks to it directly, so nothing of ours sits in between.
'telegram' is the first sending connection, and it grants a session
NOTHING: its tools list is empty on purpose, and catalog.test.ts asserts
it stays that way. A run asks to send by writing OUTBOX.json in its
sandbox; review shows the messages; approving replays them through the
bot with the token from .env — the session never holds the token and has
no tool to send with (D-075). The switch still gates it like any
credentialed connection: off, or missing its secret, means Approve
refuses with the reason. 'to' in an outbox message is a numeric chat id —
a bot can only message people who tapped Start on it once, which makes
the reachable audience exactly the people who opted in.

connections.name: web
connections.label: Read web pages
connections.description: Fetches a page and returns its readable text, trimmed. No JavaScript, no sign-ins.

connections.name: github
connections.label: Read a code host
connections.description: Reads issues, pull requests, commits and files from GitHub. Reads only — it cannot open, comment, merge or push anything.

secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN: a GitHub token with read access to the repositories the crew should see

connections.name: search
connections.label: Search the web
connections.description: Finds pages by searching, and returns titles, snippets and links. Reading one is a separate step — hand a link to the web connection.

secrets.BRAVE_API_KEY: a Brave Search API key — free tier at brave.com/search/api

connections.name: browser
connections.label: Use a web browser
connections.description: Opens pages in a real browser and reads what they show, including sites that need JavaScript. Reads only — it cannot click, type or submit anything.

connections.name: telegram
connections.label: Send Telegram messages
connections.description: Sends messages through your Telegram bot when you approve a reviewed outbox. Grants the crew no tools at all — sends happen at review, never inside a run.

secrets.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN: a bot token from @BotFather — the bot can only message people who tapped Start on it
